title: The Shoes That Waited

before.title: The Shoes That Waited
before.text: Two silver shoes wait outside Imani's door. When she puts them on, they walk toward anyone who needs help. They take her to a man with heavy bags, a lost child, and a dog behind a fence. At sunset, the shoes bring Imani home. The next morning, they are gone.

after.title: The Shoes That Waited
after.text: Two silver shoes wait outside Imani's door. When she puts them on, they walk toward someone who needs help. They take her to a man with heavy bags at the bottom of a hill. Imani offers to carry one bag. They reach his home before dark. At sunset, the shoes bring her back. She sets them beside her door, but by morning they are gone.

reason: Three people or animals needing help were introduced without outcomes. One man, one carried bag, the trip home and the shoes’ disappearance now form a complete magical sequence. Imani and the man have clear roles; the moving shoes are unmistakably fictional.

title: The Quiet Phone Basket

before.title: The Quiet Phone Basket
before.text: A family keeps looking at phones during dinner. The youngest boy puts an empty basket on the table. All agree to leave phones there for twenty minutes. At first, the room feels too quiet. Then their father tells a funny story. The basket stays on the table the next night.

after.title: The Quiet Phone Basket
after.text: A family keeps looking at phones during dinner. The youngest boy puts an empty basket on the table and asks everyone to leave their phones there for twenty minutes. They agree. At first, the room feels too quiet. Then their father tells a funny story. The basket stays on the table the next night.

reason: The boy now asks rather than silently imposing the basket. The family agrees, experiences the quiet, tells a story and chooses to repeat the activity. Short clauses and stable referents fit Level 2; this is a family story, not screen-time advice.

title: Three Bells after Closing

before.title: Three Bells after Closing
before.text: A food shop is closed, but a bell rings three times inside. A girl checks the front door. It is locked. She walks around the shop and hears the sound again. A metal tool hangs near an open window. Wind moves it against a glass. She closes the window.

after.title: Three Bells after Closing
after.text: A food shop is closed, but a bell rings three times inside. A girl checks the front door. It is locked. She walks around the shop and hears the bell again. Through an open window, she sees a small bell hanging near the frame. The wind moves it. She calls the owner, who comes to shut the window and move the bell.

reason: The sound is a real bell rather than an unexplained metal tool hitting a glass, and the girl does not enter a locked shop to close its window. The owner acts after she reports the clue. Simple clue, inspection and resolution fit Level 2.

title: Painted Doors on the Hill

before.title: Painted Doors on the Hill
before.text: This hill town is not real. Its doors have many bright colors. A guest asks why two blue doors have white circles. A woman says her family chose the sign long ago. Other homes use leaves, birds, or lines. The guest draws the doors but not the private names beside them.

after.title: Painted Doors on the Hill
after.text: This hill town is not real. Its doors have many bright colors. A guest asks why one blue door has two white circles. A woman says she and her sister painted them as stars when they moved in. Other homes have leaves or birds on their doors. The guest asks to draw her door. She agrees but asks him not to copy the family names beside it.

reason: One woman’s answer now explains the two marks instead of vaguely invoking a family sign. The visitor asks permission before drawing and respects her request about names. The town remains explicitly invented, not a claim about a real culture.

title: A Shelf for Shared Seeds

before.title: A Shelf for Shared Seeds
before.text: This library worker is not a real person. People often ask where they can share extra seeds. The worker makes one open shelf and adds small paper bags. Each bag shows the plant name and year. People take what they need and bring seeds back later. The worker checks the bags each week.

after.title: A Shelf for Shared Seeds
after.text: Mina is a fictional library worker. Visitors ask where they can share extra seeds. Mina puts a small shelf near the desk and adds paper bags. Each bag shows the plant name and year. Some visitors take seeds, and others bring more. Every week, Mina checks whether the bags still have clear labels.

reason: Replaces the nameless not-real-person preface with one explicitly fictional worker and avoids promising all borrowers return seeds. Shelf, labeled bags and weekly check give a coherent, bounded sequence; no actual library policy is asserted.

title: The Umbrella That Hated Rain

before.title: The Umbrella That Hated Rain
before.text: Nuri buys an old yellow umbrella. It opens in the sun but closes whenever rain starts. Nuri tries to fix it. Then she finds tiny seeds inside the handle. She plants them in a pot. The next week, yellow flowers open whenever drops touch them.

after.title: The Umbrella That Hated Rain
after.text: Nuri buys an old yellow umbrella. It opens in the sun but closes whenever rain starts. Nuri tries to fix it. Then she finds tiny seeds inside the handle. She plants them in a pot. The next week, yellow flowers open whenever drops touch them.

reason: The umbrella opens in sunlight but closes in rain; Nuri finds seeds inside its handle and plants them, after which flowers respond to rain. This is a deliberate fantasy reversal of an umbrella’s purpose. The pronouns and progression from object to flowers are clear and compact at Level 2; no botanical claim is implied.

title: A Quiet Town Meeting

before.title: A Quiet Town Meeting
before.text: This is a fictional town. Its public meetings are loud, so some people stop coming. The town adds a written question box and a short quiet period. People can also send ideas before the meeting. The new choices do not end every argument, but more voices enter the plan.

after.title: A Quiet Town Meeting
after.text: This town is imagined. People meet to plan a new park. Two people cannot get a word in. A clerk puts out a box for written questions. She gives everyone one quiet minute to write. At the next meeting, she reads three questions from the box. People still disagree about the park. Now the questions are part of their discussion.

reason: An invented town’s specific meeting was mislabeled explanatory nonfiction. The clerk’s action and next meeting show how written questions enter this particular discussion, without claiming that all town meetings become inclusive.

title: Toast for the Late Train

before.title: Toast for the Late Train
before.text: Jun misses his train and must wait forty minutes. He feels angry and hungry. A small cafe is still open. Jun orders toast and writes tomorrow's shopping list. When the next train comes, the wait no longer feels empty. He has eaten and finished one useful task.

after.title: Toast for the Late Train
after.text: Jun misses his train and must wait forty minutes. He feels angry and hungry. A small cafe is still open. Jun orders toast and writes tomorrow's shopping list. When the next train comes, the wait no longer feels empty. He has eaten and finished one useful task.

reason: Jun misses a train, uses the forty-minute wait for toast and a shopping list, and feels differently when the next train comes. His anger and hunger are resolved through concrete actions; the short sequence and title match. This is one fictional experience, not universal advice.

title: The Lunchbox with the Wrong Name

before.title: The Lunchbox with the Wrong Name
before.text: A boy finds his food box, but a girl's name is on it. Inside, he sees the same apple and bread that he put there. He looks under the box. His own name is on a loose strip of paper. Two food boxes had touched in a school bag, and the strips moved from one box to the other.

after.title: The Lunchbox with the Wrong Name
after.text: A boy finds his food box, but a girl's name is on its lid. Inside are the apple and bread he packed. He remembers putting his sister's box beside it in the same bag. He lifts his box and finds his own loose name label underneath. His sister's box has no label now. The two labels came loose when the boxes rubbed together, and hers stuck to his lid.

reason: The sister and the shared bag now establish why a girl’s label is present. The boy checks food, finds his own label below and sees the other lid is bare; the physical rubbing resolves the clue without changing whose lunch he has.

title: Nara Repairs One Bicycle

before.title: Nara Repairs One Bicycle
before.text: This bike worker is not a real person. She starts with one broken bike in a small shed. She tells each person what she will fix and keeps old parts that are still good. Soon, families bring bikes before school. Once a month, she shows people how to make a seat firm and put a chain back in place.

after.title: Nara Repairs One Bicycle
after.text: Nara is a fictional bicycle repair worker. She begins in a small shed with one broken bike. Before each job, she tells the owner what she plans to fix. She keeps old parts that still work. One morning, a family brings a bike with a loose seat. Nara tightens it and lets the rider check the fit. The family returns the next month with another bike.

reason: A named fictional worker replaces an unnamed biography. One repair, a rider check and a later return give a more specific outcome than a general claim that all families visit. The story does not teach a complete safety procedure.
